assumptions.subject: workload
assumptions.statement: 25,000 rps at the public edge; 5% of calls exceed quota and are rejected with 429 before reaching any upstream. 2% are key-management / token traffic.

assumptions.subject: limiter
assumptions.statement: Every request costs one Redis round trip for the token bucket - there is no cached fast path, because a stale counter is a quota bypass. This makes Redis availability a hard dependency of the whole API, not an optimisation.

assumptions.subject: keycache
assumptions.statement: 85% of calls resolve the API key from local/Redis cache; the remaining 15% hit the auth service, and 2% of API calls (1.9% of all traffic) miss through to the control-plane database.

assumptions.subject: auth
assumptions.statement: ~1,500 rps per instance: signature verification plus introspection is CPU-bound, an order of magnitude more expensive per request than routing.

assumptions.subject: gw
assumptions.statement: Keystone's grounded catalogue has NO per-instance price for a managed API gateway - AWS API Gateway bills per request, not per node - so the gateway tier reports $0 compute here. That is a stated GAP, not a free component: at 25k rps a managed gateway's per-request charge would dominate this bill. Priced as self-hosted (Envoy/Kong on your own instances), it would add roughly the same as the auth tier.

assumptions.subject: q
assumptions.statement: One metering event per request, including rejected ones - billing and abuse detection both need the 429s. That makes the event bus carry the full request rate, not the allowed rate.

_library.summary: Public API front door that authenticates callers and enforces per-key rate limits and quotas before any upstream work.
